title: Trump Calls the Press “Enemy of the People” and “Scum”
description_medium: Donald Trump repeatedly attacked journalists during his 2015–2016 campaign and first presidential term, calling the press “the enemy of the people” and describing reporters as “scum” and “sleazebags.” At rallies, he sometimes pointed out members of the press and drew boos from the crowd. He framed his criticism as a response to reporting he considered unfair or false. The supplied inauguration-day article does not substantiate every additional insult or claim about physical threats at rallies.
description_long: Trump’s hostility toward news organizations became a recurring part of his campaign appearances and public statements. During the 2016 primary campaign, he called the reporters traveling with him “scum” and “sleazebags,” and crowds often turned toward the press area to boo after he singled journalists out. In February 2017, he described major news organizations as “the enemy of the American people,” and repeated the phrase at the Conservative Political Action Conference. The Committee to Protect Journalists catalogued additional descriptions such as “human scum” and “the enemy of the people” as part of its review of Trump’s attacks on the press. Trump said he was criticizing outlets he believed published inaccurate coverage, while press-freedom advocates warned that a president’s repeated attacks could undermine public trust and intensify hostility toward reporters. These sources document a pattern of public rhetoric, but not every claimed crowd assault, death threat or foreign leader’s use of his statements as justification. Those outcomes require separate evidence. The linked inauguration article covers a separate episode and does not substantiate the full set of rally examples.
evidence_notes: New Yorker describes rally crowd reactions and epithets; CPJ compiles press attacks; TIME documents CPAC remarks. Do not assert resulting threats or violence without event-specific evidence.
corrected_wording: Proposed correction: Trump Calls the Press “Enemy of the People” and “Scum”. See evidence_notes for scope and evidentiary limits.
exact_blocker: The supplied inauguration article does not support all items in the original list (including crowd threats and foreign leaders’ justifications). This revised description covers only the sourced rhetoric and rally behavior; additional incidents need separate sources.

title: Trump Calls for ABC and NBC Licenses to Be Revoked as FCC Reviews Broadcasters
description_medium: In August 2025, Trump called on the Federal Communications Commission to revoke ABC and NBC broadcast licenses over coverage he criticized. FCC Chair Brendan Carr had launched formal reviews involving ABC, CBS, NBC, NPR and PBS. The agency licenses local broadcast stations, not the national networks themselves, though several networks own stations. The reviews intensified concerns that the administration was using regulatory scrutiny to pressure news organizations over their reporting.
description_long: In August 2025, Trump posted that ABC and NBC should face license revocation because he considered their coverage biased. FCC Chair Brendan Carr had already initiated formal reviews involving the major broadcast networks and public broadcasters, including ABC, CBS, NBC, NPR and PBS. The reviews included scrutiny of news programming and complaints about editorial choices. The FCC does not issue a single national broadcast license to ABC or NBC as corporate networks; it licenses individual local stations, some of which are owned by their parent companies. Trump’s demand targeted the network brands; the FCC’s licensing authority applies to individual broadcast stations and specific proceedings. The agency also examined separate matters involving Disney and Comcast, including corporate policies, which were not the same as reviews of news coverage. Press-freedom advocates and communications lawyers warned that politically motivated licensing threats could chill reporting, while Carr defended the FCC’s oversight role. The public record documents the demand and agency reviews, not a finding that any network violated licensing rules or a revocation of its broadcast stations’ licenses. The episode raised a conflict between regulatory authority and editorial independence.
evidence_notes: NPR distinguishes national networks from individually licensed local stations and reports reviews. Trump demanded revocation; no license was revoked.
corrected_wording: Proposed correction: Trump Calls for ABC and NBC Licenses to Be Revoked as FCC Reviews Broadcasters. See evidence_notes for scope and evidentiary limits.

title: Patel’s Public Threat Against Journalists Does Not Establish an FBI Surveillance List
description_medium: The supplied NBC report describes Kash Patel’s public statement that he would pursue media figures he believed had broken the law. It does not report that the FBI created a surveillance list of journalists, monitored their communications or warned reporters that they were being tracked. Those are operational claims beyond the linked account.
description_long: Before his confirmation as FBI director, Kash Patel discussed pursuing journalists and other media figures whom he believed had committed crimes. The supplied NBC report covers those public remarks and their context in Patel’s nomination. It does not identify an FBI surveillance list, a bureau program targeting journalists because of their reporting, or specific reporters whose communications were monitored. Separate historical cases in which federal prosecutors obtained journalists’ records during leak investigations are not proof that Patel created the program alleged in this entry. The FBI’s use of subpoenas and surveillance authorities is governed by distinct legal and departmental procedures, and identifying a particular list or monitoring operation would require records, named targets or reporting tied to the alleged activity. No such operational evidence is included in the packet. Patel’s public threat may be documented as political rhetoric, but it cannot establish that the bureau carried it out through a surveillance system. The record’s central claim remains unverified without an event-specific source describing the list’s creation, purpose, participants and use.
evidence_notes: NBC reports Patel’s 2023 public comments; AP concerns historical DOJ leak investigations. Neither substantiates a Kash Patel-era journalist surveillance list.
corrected_wording: Proposed correction: Patel’s Public Threat Against Journalists Does Not Establish an FBI Surveillance List. See evidence_notes for scope and evidentiary limits.
exact_blocker: No source identifies an FBI surveillance list targeting journalists or reports monitoring their communications. The linked NBC article documents Patel’s public rhetoric only; an operational source naming the list or program is required.

title: Trump Demands Retraction from The New York Times and Threatens Suit Over Iran Reporting
description_medium: In June 2025, Trump’s lawyer demanded that The New York Times retract and apologize for reporting on an early intelligence assessment of U.S. strikes on Iranian nuclear sites, threatening a defamation lawsuit. Trump also threatened legal action against CNN over related coverage. The reports contradicted his claim that the strikes had completely destroyed Iran’s nuclear capabilities. The supplied source does not substantiate additional threats against The Washington Post, antitrust action or IRS audits.
description_long: After U.S. strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities in June 2025, preliminary intelligence reporting said the damage may have set back Iran’s nuclear program by months rather than destroying it. Trump disputed those accounts. His personal attorney sent The New York Times a letter demanding a retraction and apology and threatening a defamation suit over its reporting. Trump also threatened to sue CNN over related coverage and publicly called for reporters to be fired. Both outlets stood by their reporting. These demands were private legal threats and public statements; they did not amount to a court finding that either outlet had published false information. The episode drew concern from press-freedom advocates because a president was using litigation threats against media organizations over coverage of military operations and intelligence. Reporting on the dispute describes demands directed to The New York Times and CNN. Claims about The Washington Post, antitrust investigations, broadcast-license challenges or IRS audits require separate dated evidence.
evidence_notes: NYT/Mediaite describe demands to NYT and CNN; outlets stood by the reporting. No supporting source found for WaPo, antitrust or IRS threats in this event.
corrected_wording: Proposed correction: limit title and description to the documented retraction demand to The New York Times and legal threat to CNN over Iran-strike reporting.
exact_blocker: The linked report substantiates demands to The New York Times and threats against CNN, but does not establish parallel Washington Post demands or threatened antitrust, license or IRS actions.

title: Trump Threatens Prosecution of Journalists Over Iran Intelligence Leak
description_medium: In a June 29, 2025, interview, Trump said his administration was considering forcing journalists to identify sources who leaked an intelligence assessment of U.S. strikes on Iran and suggested reporters could be prosecuted. The assessment said the strikes had set back Iran’s nuclear program but did not establish that it was destroyed. Trump accused Democrats of leaking the information. The remarks raised questions about press protections and government efforts to compel disclosure of confidential sources.
description_long: Trump made the remarks during a June 29, 2025, interview with Fox News host Maria Bartiromo, after outlets reported on a preliminary Defense Intelligence Agency assessment of the U.S. strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities. That assessment suggested the strikes had caused damage but may have delayed Iran’s nuclear program by months rather than eliminating it. Trump said he was considering whether to require journalists who published details from the report to reveal their sources and suggested that reporters and sources could face prosecution if they did not comply. He separately accused Democrats of leaking the information. The statements were not an indictment or court order compelling a reporter to disclose a source; they described possible steps under consideration. Press-freedom advocates warned that using prosecution threats to identify confidential sources could deter reporting on national-security matters. Federal law offers journalists limited and context-dependent protections, and no universal federal shield law prevents every demand for source disclosure. The event concerned coverage of classified intelligence about a military operation, with the administration asserting a national-security interest and journalists invoking the public’s interest in scrutiny of government claims. The threats did not themselves result in a reported conviction or source disclosure.
evidence_notes: Guardian reports the June 29 interview and stated possibility of compelling journalists or prosecuting sources/reporters. Distinguish consideration and threat from an actual order or prosecution.
corrected_wording: Proposed correction: Trump Threatens Prosecution of Journalists Over Iran Intelligence Leak. See evidence_notes for scope and evidentiary limits.

title: Trump Demands Journalists Return “Noble” Prizes for Russia Reporting
description_medium: On April 26, 2020, Trump tweeted that journalists who received “Noble Prizes” for reporting on Russia should return them. The awards he meant were Pulitzers, not Nobel Prizes, and his message appeared during a series of posts attacking coverage of the Russia investigation. He later asked whether his use of “Noble” was understood as sarcasm. No prize was revoked, and the award organizations did not act on his demand.
description_long: Trump’s April 26, 2020, social-media posts attacked journalists who had received awards for reporting on Russian interference in the 2016 election. He wrote that reporters who had received “Noble Prizes” for their work should return them so they could be given to “real reporters.” Journalists covering the Russia investigation had received Pulitzer Prizes; the Nobel Prize is a separate award and is not given for journalism. After the wording drew attention, Trump tweeted, “Does anybody get the meaning of what a so-called Noble (not Nobel) Prize is, especially as it pertains to Reporters and Journalists?” He later asked whether sarcasm worked. The remarks were part of his broader effort to discredit reporting on Russian election interference and the Mueller investigation. They did not initiate a formal review by the Pulitzer organization, and no award was taken away. This episode is distinct from later controversies about Pulitzer awards and should not be described as Trump demanding that a Nobel committee revoke a journalist’s Nobel Prize. The documented target was journalists’ Pulitzer recognition, with Trump’s phrasing playing on the similar-sounding word “Noble.”
evidence_notes: Washington Post documents exact posts and correction from Nobel to Pulitzer. Separate from the linked 2022 Pulitzer story and no Nobel prize was revoked.
corrected_wording: Proposed correction: change the event date to April 26, 2020, and describe the “Noble”/Pulitzer tweet rather than a demand to revoke a Nobel Prize.

title: Trump Blames Antifa and “Radical Left” for Protest Violence
description_medium: In a June 1, 2020, statement following protests over George Floyd’s killing, Trump said the country had been gripped by “professional anarchists,” “violent mobs,” “Antifa” and other groups. He characterized the unrest as coordinated violence rather than solely peaceful protest and threatened to deploy military forces if state and local governments failed to restore order. The statement did not establish that Antifa organized the protests, and Trump did not invoke the Insurrection Act that day.
description_long: Trump issued a statement on June 1, 2020, as demonstrations following George Floyd’s killing spread across the United States. He said that “professional anarchists,” “violent mobs,” looters, rioters, Antifa and others had gripped the country, and described the events as more than peaceful protests. In a televised address that evening, he said he would deploy the military and invoke the Insurrection Act if governors and mayors did not control the unrest. Federal law-enforcement officials had not publicly produced evidence that Antifa centrally coordinated the nationwide protests; Antifa is a loose movement rather than a single national organization. Trump’s claims therefore represented his characterization of demonstrators and violence, not an established finding of a centralized conspiracy. Earlier that day, federal officers cleared protesters from Lafayette Square before Trump walked to St. John’s Church. The White House said the area was cleared for security and access; the operation’s timing and purpose were disputed. The June 1 remarks intensified debate over protest rights, public order and the use of federal troops domestically. Trump did not formally invoke the Insurrection Act during this episode.
evidence_notes: White House statement supports rhetoric; senators sought evidence for Antifa claims. Insurrection Act threat was separate and no invocation occurred; Lafayette Square operation not attributed to a motive.
corrected_wording: Proposed correction: Trump Blames Antifa and “Radical Left” for Protest Violence. See evidence_notes for scope and evidentiary limits.

title: Infants and Toddlers Held in “Tender Age” Shelters After Family Separation
description_medium: During the 2018 family-separation policy, infants and toddlers separated from parents at the U.S.-Mexico border were placed in shelters run for unaccompanied children. Lawyers and medical providers described young children crying inconsolably and showing distress in a Rio Grande Valley shelter. Pediatricians warned that separation from caregivers could harm children’s health and development. The available reporting supports the shelter placements and observed distress, but does not establish every claim about abuse by staff or children who were not reunited after court orders.
description_long: In June 2018, reports emerged that very young children separated from their parents at the U.S.-Mexico border were being housed in facilities intended for unaccompanied minors. Associated Press reporters described a shelter in the Rio Grande Valley where lawyers and medical providers saw toddlers in emotional distress, including children crying and calling for their parents. The placements followed the administration’s “zero tolerance” prosecution policy, under which parents were detained for criminal immigration proceedings and children were transferred to the Office of Refugee Resettlement. An inspector general report later described problems caused by family separations and the difficulty of identifying and tracking all separated children. The American Academy of Pediatrics warned that separation from a primary caregiver could cause serious developmental and psychological harm, especially for infants and toddlers. President Trump signed an executive order on June 20, 2018, directing agencies to maintain family unity where legally possible, and a federal court later ordered reunifications. These sources document the separation, shelter conditions and medical concerns. They do not verify the synopsis’s separate allegations that staff inappropriately touched children or that many remained separated despite specific court orders; those claims require individual investigations and records. The reports document young children’s treatment during the 2018 policy; later reunification cases require separate records.
evidence_notes: AP/Guardian report describes the Rio Grande Valley tender-age shelter. HHS OIG documents policy and tracking problems; AAP warning reported. Abuse and individual reunification claims remain unverified.
corrected_wording: Proposed correction: Infants and Toddlers Held in “Tender Age” Shelters After Family Separation. See evidence_notes for scope and evidentiary limits.
exact_blocker: The packet’s allegations about staff abuse and failures to reunite children under specific court orders lack case-level sources; this partial description covers supported placements and distress only.
